paper_title: SepLLM Accelerate Large Language Models by Compressing One Segment into   One Separator
caption_used: Training loss curves over iterations for Vanilla, StrmLLM (n=64), and four SepLLM configurations. All models start with loss values exceeding 3.4 and converge as training progresses to 140,000 iterations. The Vanilla model achieves the lowest final loss at approximately 2.45, while StrmLLM (n=64) converges to roughly 2.60, showing a notable gap from the SepLLM variants. Among the SepLLM configurations, the H/T variant reaches the lowest loss at approximately 2.49, with SepLLM (n=128) settling at approximately 2.55, slightly above both the base SepLLM (n=64) and SepLLM (n=64, H) which converge near 2.51-2.52. The most rapid decrease in loss occurs within the first 20,000 iterations for all models, after which convergence slows considerably.
model_annotation: This plot illustrates the training loss curves for five different language model configurations over a range of 140,000 iterations. The x-axis, labeled "#Iteration", is linear and spans from 0 to 140,000. The y-axis, labeled "Loss", is also linear and ranges from 2.4 to 3.4. The plot displays five lines: the "Vanilla" model (purple, solid line), "StrmLLM (n=64)" (blue, solid line), "SepLLM (n=64)" (orange, solid line), "SepLLM (n=64, H)" (green, solid line), "SepLLM (n=64, H/T)" (red, solid line), and "SepLLM (n=128)" (dark blue, solid line). All lines begin at a loss value above 3.4 and decrease over time. The "Vanilla" model starts at approximately 3.4 and ends at approximately 2.45. The "StrmLLM (n=64)" model starts at approximately 3.4 and ends at approximately 2.60. The "SepLLM (n=64)" model starts at approximately 3.4 and ends at approximately 2.51. The "SepLLM (n=64, H)" model starts at approximately 3.4 and ends at approximately 2.52. The "SepLLM (n=64, H/T)" model starts at approximately 3.4 and ends at approximately 2.49. The "SepLLM (n=128)" model starts at approximately 3.4 and ends at approximately 2.55. All curves exhibit a steep initial decline, particularly within the first 20,000 iterations, followed by a gradual flattening as they approach their final loss values.
